articleTitle: The content and organisation of user documentation for information systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Issues in Computer Support for Documentation and Manuals
abstract: The problems of organising information within user documentation (both power and online) have grown along with software complexity. The author discusses problems in documenting navigation routes, cross references and functions with a long scope of interaction, encountered during a large commercial user documentation project. These problems need to be addressed by tools providing computer support for documentation and manuals.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Issues in Computer Support for Documentation and Manuals
abstract: Two forms of quick reference (QR) documentation discussed are syntax summaries and quick reference guides. Syntax summaries typically list tasks or commands in alphabetical order, often on a single sheet or card (for example, the action to bold text is press SHIFT+B). Quick reference guides contain more extended procedures and often come in booklets (for example, giving a four step procedure to set up columns in a document). QR documentation is usually regraded more as a reference than a learning tool more for memory jogging than for initial learning. However, the author looks at the learning function and analyses it using the minimalist model developed by J.M. Carroll (1990).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: System documentation and system design: a good reason for designing the manual first
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Issues in Computer Support for Documentation and Manuals
abstract: The usability of systems has become an increasingly important issue in the design and implementation of systems. Usability can be defined in terms of four basic criteria: effectiveness, learnability, flexibility and attitude. The author argues for user centred design and suggests that a major benefit to the design process can be obtained if system documentation is treated as a component of user centred design and as such 'put to work' in the design of the system. The following stages should be adopted: the data obtained in the user requirements analysis (the requirements report) should be written as a prototype user manual and made available to users immediately for comments and evaluation, and user comments should be used to re-write the manual (iteration); the three stage design documents and screen design should be incorporated into the user manual and users asked to comment as part of the evaluation process and again iteration should take place; and when the first prototype is available for 'hands-on' evaluation the user manual should be evaluated with the software-any changes made to the software should also be reflected in the manual.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Database support for the production of reusable technical documentation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Issues in Computer Support for Documentation and Manuals
abstract: The approach to the production of technical documentation described arose from a need to supply documentation for a large library of mathematical software. There has been a growing demand to supply documentation in a variety of printed and online formats, tailored to the particular needs of end users. There is also an increasing number of new products which contain the original library as an embedded sub-component. First attempts to meet the demand for diverse forms of documentation led to the creation of many different bodies of text, containing similar information, but maintained and often authored separately. The solution to this problem was to develop a database which contains all the information previously held in the library documentation. The database can be used to generate both the original documents and new documents with varying style, format or content. There were two main processes involved in the transformation of documents to database records. The first was an object-oriented decomposition of the documented product, identifying all the sub-components and the important information relating to each one. The second process was to mark up text records using the Standard Generalized Markup Language (SGML), an ISO standard (8879) for the mark up of computer-held documents.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A natural interface to on-line documentation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Issues in Computer Support for Documentation and Manuals
abstract: Proverbial wisdom suggests that reading manuals is the naturally least favoured method for understanding how to manipulate a mechanism with success. It is therefore surprising that help systems should be regarded as an essential feature of a person-oriented computer system. However, it is accepted that in order to learn how, for example, to express oneself in Z or to determine what is the order of the parameters in a procedure call, documents need to be read. So online help systems should describe the task rather than the means by which the task is done. Since the information may express difficult concepts, the user interface that enables the person to access that information should cause th minimum of cognitive interference. Conventional hypertext based systems, through technically powerful, unfortunately require significant cognitive effort to be expanded on their manipulation and their display metaphors are based on those that pre-date books. An alternative vehicle for accessing information is described in three variations. The vehicle exploits a book metaphor for its display: an evolutionary step which closely follows that through which paper-based methods passed. The result is familiar and comfortable.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Hyperusing: hypertext as combined system and manual
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Issues in Computer Support for Documentation and Manuals
abstract: It is easier to understand the ideas introduced by first showing some of the features of a simple system that has been implemented. This introduction is followed by a more conceptual discussion, which emphasises the generality and power of the examples used. The system is currently called Hyperdoc. Hyperdoc can run any finite state machine (up to a large size), and combines it with its manual. Hyperdoc is implemented by HyperCard. Hyperdoc provides a point-and-click user interface to whatever system it is simulating.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Identifying the role of hypertext in the computing paradigm
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Issues in Computer Support for Documentation and Manuals
abstract: Hypertext and hypermedia are technologies that have evolved to illustrate a class of computer based solutions rather than as solutions to specified, well defined problems. Now that usable technology is emerging much attention is being directed towards identifying problems that such systems could address. The study is concerned with identifying some of the factors prohibiting the introduction of electronic documentation. The focus of the study is the production of an 'electronic laboratory hand book' for use in a district general hospital.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer support for documentation consistency maintenance
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Issues in Computer Support for Documentation and Manuals
abstract: Consideration is given to computer-based techniques for maintaining the internal consistency of documentation in the face of modifications. The author argues that the dependencies between parts of the documentation are an important aspect of the maintenance problem. Techniques for identifying and maintaining dependencies have been implemented in a prototype editor, called HyDIE. Within HyDIE, all documents are represented in terms of their logical structure. The notion of a logical document model underpins both the SGML and ODA document standards. To support an author in identifying dependent parts, HyDIE provides a hypertext linking facility comprising both explicit links and automatically generated links, which usually involve search of some kind.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer aided documentation for software maintenance
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Issues in Computer Support for Documentation and Manuals
abstract: Upon inspection much of the documentation that exists for software applications is either associated with its design or its user interface i.e. reference manuals and user guides. Little, if any documentation, is specifically produced to help those who are involved with looking after the application once it is released to its users, and enters its maintenance phase. If such documentation does exist it is often found not to accurately represent the current state of the application. As a solution, the author suggests the use of code documentation tools. These tools can provide those involved with looking after existing applications with virtual information, and the mechanism for keeping notes about them. In the same way that a carpenter or a plumber needs the right tools to complete their jobs, those working in maintaining software need tools to help them perform their tasks in an effective manner. Code documentation tools are now available which can not only aid the extraction and analysis of existing applications, but provide accurate information in a form that is easy to understand, interactive in use, and most importantly is shareable by all those needed to work on the project.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Issues in Computer Support for Documentation and Manuals
abstract: The widespread availability of low-cost, high performance, multimedia personal computer systems makes possible many new types of documentation and support methods for handling it. The authors outline some of the research into potential applications of linear and nonlinear multimedia documentation within the framework of electronic performance support systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Issues in Computer Support for Documentation and Manuals
abstract: Document management can be addressed at many levels, and degrees of sophistication, from personal to corporate systems using a variety of standard and customised solutions. Recognition is increasing that documents are a vital business asset, deserving the necessary investment. Electronic reference documents are a practical method of publishing complex information and maintaining its currency and integrity. The key to success is recognising the various data requirements, and using an appropriate database and application technology. Kinesis' Total Recall system offers a unique and virtual foundation to a document management system to enrich existing solutions and as a platform for high-performance applications. Total Recall was developed by integrating the requirements of many clients and provides an online engineering reference manual for a major utility company.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
